title: Death at the Lighthouse
setting: Gallows Point Lighthouse, a storm-battered rock off the coast of Maine, 1931. The supply boat won't return until morning.
intro: Keeper Elias Morrow invited a handful of guests to watch the lamp being lit for the last time before the lighthouse is decommissioned. The waves are high. The lamp is turning. Something is wrong.

victim.name: Elias Morrow
victim.description: The old lighthouse keeper. Gruff, superstitious, and sitting on a secret about a shipwreck forty years ago.

rounds.title: Round 1 — The Lamp Goes Dark
rounds.narration: At nine o'clock the great lamp sputters and dies. In the blackness you hear a scream from the gallery above — and a heavy thud on the iron stairs. When the lamp flickers back to life, Elias Morrow lies at the bottom of the spiral staircase, neck broken, a brass key clutched in his fist.
rounds.publicText: The keeper is dead at the foot of the stairs, a brass key in his hand. No boat until dawn. Talk to each other.

rounds.title: Round 2 — The Gallery Argument
rounds.narration: The gallery where Elias fell was also the place where Nell argued with him about selling the land. She has debts; the doctor has private knowledge; the assistant knows the lamp. Each connection sounds worse in the darkness. But bruises shaped like hands make this more than an ordinary fall, and the lamp failed at the moment a push could be hidden.
rounds.publicText: The argument, private warning and lamp access implicate different people. Establish the method before treating a motive as proof.
rounds.hostNotes: Read every public clue, discuss, then vote.

rounds.title: Round 3 — The Logbook
rounds.narration: Someone finds the keeper's logbook. The final entry, written tonight, reads: 'One of them knows what happened to the Mary Celeste II. I will tell the coast guard at dawn.'
rounds.publicText: The logbook names no one — but the keeper meant to talk at dawn. Share your secrets.
rounds.hostNotes: Compare the threatened shipwreck disclosure with the earlier property argument, then vote.

rounds.title: Round 4 — Two Different Secrets
rounds.narration:
Elias's last written threat concerns a shipwreck, not the sale of the land. The niece's argument and the doctor's silence remain uncomfortable, but discomfort is not a single explanation of this death. The doctor kept a warning because admitting it would expose how long she had withheld it. Nell wanted money from a sale, not the buried shipwreck story.

Keep the earlier accusations beside these corrections. Neither is an invented alibi. Ask which explanation also accounts for the lamp's failure, the stained sleeve and the climb just before darkness.
rounds.publicText: The logbook weakens the property theory. The warning explains the doctor's secrecy; it does not identify a medical cause of death. Test the blackout timeline.
rounds.hostNotes: Let players revisit their earlier votes using the corrections.

rounds.title: Round 5 — The Other Key
rounds.narration:
The brass key in Elias's hand opens the oil store. Wick has the only other copy. The doctor's account of Elias's warning names Wick's father as the man behind the wreck and says the son knew Elias had seen it.

Put that account beside the stair sighting and oil-stained sleeve. The lamp failed, the gallery went dark, and Elias was pushed. A disputed inheritance and an embarrassing silence explain why other guests looked guilty; the same chain must explain the threatened disclosure and the opportunity on the stairs.
rounds.publicText: The key, warning, oil and stair sighting must fit one account of motive, method and opportunity.
rounds.hostNotes: Final round: read every clue, vote, then reveal.

characters.name: Nell Harrow
characters.publicBlurb: Elias's niece and only family. Arrived late on the last boat, smelling of wine.
characters.backstory: You came to beg your uncle to sell the lighthouse land. He refused.
secrets: You argued with Elias on the gallery an hour before he died.

readAloud.text: {wick} climbed the stairs just before the lamp died. Lamp oil stains the assistant keeper's sleeve: why was he near the gallery when he claims he stayed in the oil store?

clues: You argued with Elias about selling the land; you fear that makes you look guilty.

readAloud.text: {doc} knew Elias feared someone on the island but kept the warning private. The doctor visited him repeatedly; that silence could protect a reputation or conceal a more personal interest.

clues: Your property argument took place an hour before the lamp failed, not at the moment of the push.

readAloud.text: {wick} says he stayed in the oil store alone. That account conflicts with the stair sighting immediately before darkness. The logbook's threatened shipwreck disclosure now makes the timing important, not just the stained sleeve.

clues: The keeper's brass key is connected to the oil store.

readAloud.text: {doc} kept a warning about a shipwreck, not a medical treatment. Hand-shaped bruises support a push, not a death from the keeper's failing health. The doctor's shame explains withheld information but does not explain the lamp going dark.

clues: The logbook concerns the shipwreck, not your proposal to sell the land.

readAloud.text: {wick} has the only other oil-store key. Elias's warning named Wick's father as the man who sank the ship; exposure was due at dawn. The key, oil-stained sleeve and stair sighting connect motive, blackout and opportunity.

clues: The brass key opens the oil store; Wick has the only other copy.

characters.name: Jonah Wick
characters.publicBlurb: Elias's taciturn assistant for ten years.
characters.backstory: Forty years ago your father wrecked the Mary Celeste II for the insurance money. Elias saw it happen.
secrets: YOU ARE THE KILLER. You may lie.
You cut the lamp's oil line and pushed Elias down the stairs in the dark.
characters.motive: Elias was going to expose your family's crime at dawn.

readAloud.text: {doc} knew Elias's health and had private visits with him. Elias said he feared someone on the island, yet the doctor kept that warning quiet. Why?

clues: There is lamp oil on your sleeve. You may lie in discussion, but read your public clue in full.

readAloud.text: {nell} argued with Elias on the gallery and inherits the land. The debts make the quarrel more than a passing disagreement; she wanted him to agree to a sale.

clues: Your claimed oil-store alibi is false.

readAloud.text: {doc} could have passed on the private warning before tonight. The logbook says disclosure was due at dawn; the delay leaves the doctor's account needing an explanation.

clues: The logbook threatens to expose your family's shipwreck crime.

readAloud.text: {nell} inherits the land and argued for a sale, but Elias's logbook threatens to expose a shipwreck, not a property dispute. The argument happened an hour before the blackout. Those corrections weaken the earlier accusation without pretending the debts disappeared.

clues: The niece's argument cannot explain your oil-stained sleeve or the stair sighting.

readAloud.text: {doc} withheld Elias's warning to protect a reputation, then supplied its shipwreck account. The bruises establish the push and the account supplies the threatened disclosure. Medical access alone cannot explain the oil-store key and lamp failure.

clues: You may challenge interpretations in discussion, but read the public clue in full.

characters.name: Dr. Ruth Calder
characters.publicBlurb: A doctor visiting from the mainland to check on the keeper's failing health.
characters.backstory: You have been treating Elias for months. He confided in you. You feared that exposing his warning would also expose how long you had kept silent.
secrets: Elias told you he was afraid of someone on the island.
characters.motive: Protect your reputation from questions about the warning you withheld.

readAloud.text: {nell} argued with Elias on the gallery an hour before he died. Debts and the inheritance give the niece a reason to want the land, while hand-shaped bruises show someone pushed him.

clues: The keeper's death was not an accidental fall.

readAloud.text: {wick} worked with the lamp and has oil on his sleeve. The failure supplied darkness for a push. An assistant's routine work might explain a stain, but it must also explain the movement on the stairs.

clues: You withheld Elias's warning because you feared questions about your silence.

readAloud.text: {nell} wanted the land sold, while Elias's final logbook entry concerns an old shipwreck. The written threat tests whether the property quarrel actually explains why he had to die before dawn.

clues: Elias's written threat confirms that he meant to talk about the shipwreck.

readAloud.text: {wick} claims an oil-store alibi, but was seen climbing just before the blackout. No correction to the niece's property motive or the doctor's silence removes that conflict. The lamp access must fit the sighting.

clues: The hand-shaped bruises separate this crime from the keeper's illness.

readAloud.text: {nell} had a financial motive, but her earlier argument does not account for the shipwreck warning, the darkened lamp and the assistant's contradictory movements. Her debt is real; it is not a substitute for a connected account of the push.

clues: Elias told you: 'Wick's father sank that ship, and the boy knows I saw.'

finale.narration: The lamp turns. The sea roars. Who pushed Elias Morrow down the stairs?

solution.explanation: Jonah Wick cut the oil line to darken the lamp, climbed the stairs (seen by Nell), and pushed Elias, who was about to expose the wreck of the Mary Celeste II. The oil on his sleeve and the doctor's testimony seal it.
solution.revealNarration: Jonah Wick stares at the oil on his sleeve. 'He should have taken it to his grave,' he whispers. 'Now he has.'
